home.meta_title: IRAI — Swarms of societies of swarms
home.meta_desc: IRAI measures how many independent opinions your AI swarm holds, and helps you get more. Swarms of societies of swarms.
hero.canvas_aria: Animation of agent answers scattered around a true value. The more the agents' errors correlate, the tighter they clump and the further the crowd's average lands from the truth.
hero.fallback_aria: Drawing of agent answers scattered around a true value: swarms grouped into societies of swarms, their average landing away from the truth.
hero.lede: Copies of one model make the same mistakes. We measure how many independent opinions your AI swarm holds, and help you get more.
hero.rho_label: How alike are the agents' errors? {rho} = {value}
hero.error_left: Error left after averaging: {pct} of one agent's
hero.live.one: {n} agents with error correlation {rho} are worth about {k} independent opinion.
hero.live.other: {n} agents with error correlation {rho} are worth about {k} independent opinions.
ceiling.h2: Past a point, more agents add nothing
ceiling.p1: When agents share their mistakes, what the crowd is worth levels off. At an error correlation of 0.25 the ceiling is four independent judges, whether you run fifty agents or fifty thousand.
ceiling.p2: We first ran into this in our own experiment. One LLM agent outscored every person in the room, and the crowd of people still outscored every crowd of agents. Other groups report the same limit in model ensembles and LLM judge panels.
ceiling.cite_html: Salles & Graeml, Echoes of Humanity (AMCIS 2026). Lefort et al. (2024). Abels & Lenaerts (IJCAI 2025). Kohli (2026, preprint).
ceiling.fig_h: Independent judges a swarm is worth
ceiling.fig_sub: by number of agents, at three levels of error correlation
chart.aria: Line chart. With no error correlation every agent counts. At correlation 0.05 a swarm levels off near 20 independent judges, at 0.25 near 4, at 0.5 near 2, however many agents are added.
do.neff.q: How many independent judges are in your agent fleet?
do.neff.p: Send us your swarm's outputs. We report its error correlation and effective crowd size, prescribe the cheapest fix, and measure again.
do.neff.for: For teams running judge panels, agent fleets and ensembles
do.society.q: A synthetic population of Brazil, scored against real outcomes.
do.society.p: The population comes from public TSE and IBGE data. Language models only supply how each kind of person is likely to choose, and every forecast is checked against published results.
do.society.for: For research and polling firms, brands, banks and policy teams
do.prova.q: Test a product concept on a synthetic panel before you pay for a human one.
do.prova.p: Synthetic consumers built from Brazilian census profiles read your concept and say in their own words whether they'd buy it. We turn those words into purchase-intent ratings and show you the reasons behind them.
do.prova.for: For consumer goods, retail and research firms screening concepts
do.guarda.p: One injected sentence can flip every agent of a lineage at once. Guarda tracks correlated failure, collusion and monoculture exposure across the whole swarm.
do.guarda.for: For AI lab evaluation teams, security teams and regulators
ladder.h2: Crowd wisdom has to be built
ladder.p1: People in a crowd each know something the others don't. Agents built on one model all know the same things.
ladder.p2: Here are eight ways to change that, shallowest first. Our research ranks them by how much each one lowers error correlation per dollar.
ladder.0.p: Temperature and seeds. Noise around one shared belief.
ladder.1.p: Expert roles and demographic prompts. Cheap, and prone to caricature.
ladder.2.p: Base rates, checklists, counterfactuals, red-team framing.
ladder.3.p: Different providers, corpora and languages. Sabiá beside GPT beside Gemini.
ladder.4.p: Each agent sees a different slice of the evidence.
ladder.5.p: Different search engines, databases or document sets per agent.
ladder.7.p: Agents conditioned on real people's interviews or answers.
ladder.note: We're testing a ninth rung, activation steering, which shifts how a model reasons without retraining it. The open question is whether it buys as much independence as a second lineage, and at what cost.
manifesto.mission: We started this company to answer one question: how many minds are in the swarm?
manifesto.letter1: We kept meeting teams who added agents and got the same answer back, only louder. Run one model a thousand times and you still have one opinion.
manifesto.letter2: An iraí colony gets by on small bees doing different jobs. We build agent swarms the same way, and we check our work with numbers.
manifesto.dusk_aria: Animation: bees zigzag home to a round nest entrance while a few guards hover beside it.
products.meta_title: Products: Neff Audit, Model Society, Prova and Guarda — IRAI
products.meta_desc: Neff Audit, Model Society, Prova and Guarda: count the independent judges in your agent fleet, simulate Brazil, screen product concepts and monitor the swarm.
products.lede: Keep whatever agent framework you already run. We measure how well the agents on it think as a group, and we improve that.
products.neff.intro: You run many agents because many opinions should beat one. The audit tells you how many opinions you're paying for and how many you're getting.
products.neff.d1.p: Pairwise correlation of your agents' errors, within and across models, prompts and tools.
products.neff.d2.p: The number of independent judges your swarm is worth.
products.neff.d3.p: How much of the crowd's gain comes from member competence and how much from their disagreement.
products.neff.d4.p: Tokens, money and estimated energy for each answer, against a single-call baseline.
products.neff.s1.p: Agent or judge outputs on a labelled task set. We don't need your prompts or weights.
products.neff.s2.p: Correlation matrix, effective size, discrimination and calibration.
products.neff.s3.p: The cheapest lever that adds independence: a second lineage, partitioned evidence, a different aggregation rule.
products.neff.s4.p: The same metrics after the change, so the gain is on paper.
products.society.intro: A synthetic population of Brazil that starts from the real electorate and consumer base, and is scored against outcomes anyone can check. Latin America comes next.
products.society.d1.p: Registered voters by section from the TSE, joined to IBGE Census 2022. The models never invent who lives where.
products.society.d2.p: The probability that a given kind of person makes a given choice. Turnout and population counts stay empirical, so every error can be traced to its source.
products.society.d3.p: Post-stratification carries those probabilities to any level where the population mix is known: state, municipality, polling place, voting section.
products.society.d4.p: Small units are noisy by nature. We report skill above a uniform-swing baseline at every level and say where it peaks.
products.society.d5.p: Portuguese-native models such as Sabiá and Lumi run beside global ones. We report where their errors cancel and where they share blind spots.
products.society.d6.p: Before trusting what a model says about a place, we probe what it knows about that place and shrink the rest to zero.
products.society.note: Model Society outputs are synthetic simulations, never electoral polls. We release nothing about an election before polls close, and we don't publish synthetic voter quotes or portraits of small identifiable communities.
products.prova.intro: Concept tests ask a panel how likely they are to buy, on a five-point scale. Language models asked for that number directly give the safe answer: mostly 3, almost never 1 or 5. Prova asks for words instead and measures where they fall on the scale.
products.prova.d1.p: Each synthetic consumer gets a persona and the concept, as an image or as text, and writes a short statement of purchase intent.
products.prova.d2.p_html: We embed each statement and compare it with reference statements for each point on the scale. The result is a distribution over 1 to 5, not a single number. The method comes from Maier et al. (2025, preprint), who report about 90% of human test–retest reliability across 57 personal care surveys.
products.prova.d3.p: Panels are drawn from IBGE census profiles, the same frame as Model Society. Without demographic personas the ratings come out uniformly positive and the ranking signal drops.
products.prova.d4.p: Every study reports distribution similarity and how much of the test–retest ceiling of your own past human panels the synthetic panel reaches.
products.prova.d5.p: Every rating comes with the statement that produced it, so objections and selling points can be read and grouped.
products.prova.d6.h: More than one mind on the panel
products.prova.d6.p: We run the panel across model lineages and report its effective size, so you know how many independent opinions it holds.
products.prova.s1.p: Concept boards or descriptions, and past human results if you have them.
products.prova.s2.p: Reference statements and personas are checked against your past studies.
products.prova.s3.p: Purchase-intent distributions, concept ranking and the reasons behind them.
products.prova.s4.p: Decide which concepts are worth a human panel.
products.prova.note: Prova screens concepts; it doesn't replace a human panel. It works where models have seen people discuss the category, and it is weaker for subgroups such as gender and region. We say which, per study.
products.guarda.intro: Most monitoring watches one agent and its permissions. Guarda watches what a group of agents does together. It's named for the guard bees that hover at a stingless-bee nest entrance.
products.guarda.d1.p: Alerts when agents start failing on the same items at the same time. That usually means a shared blind spot or a shared attack.
products.guarda.d2.p: Coordination between agents that the task didn't ask for, tracked as a property of the swarm.
products.guarda.d3.p: How much of your swarm one prompt injection could flip, by lineage.
products.guarda.d4.p: Trimmed and Byzantine-robust rules in place of a plain median, so a compromised lineage can't carry the vote.
research.meta_desc: IRAI's research programme on the collective intelligence of LLM agent swarms: open questions, the measurement kit, papers, and the rules we hold ourselves to.
research.lede: We study how the collective intelligence of human crowds does and doesn't emerge in swarms of language models, and what it takes to build it on purpose.
research.q1.p: Rank sampling, persona, reasoning strategy, lineage, information partition, tools and weights on one task, in error-correlation terms, per dollar.
research.q2.p: Where activation steering sits between a persona prompt and a fine-tuned adapter.
research.q3.p: How much evidence agents should share. Too little and nobody can cross-check; too much and they're redundant.
research.q4.p: Correlated attacks and emergent coordination as measurable swarm properties.
research.q5.p: A Local Knowledge Index per place and model, and a skill-by-scale curve from state down to voting section.
research.q6.p: Whether semantic similarity rating holds for Brazilian consumers, answers written in Portuguese, and categories models have seen less of.
research.q7.p: When people and agents make different kinds of errors, and how to pool them.
research.q8.p: Accuracy per joule, against the single-call baseline.
research.kit.p: Every study and every audit reports the same five things, so results can be compared across tasks.
research.k1.p: The average pairwise correlation of agents' errors, written {rho}, reported within and across each diversity lever.
research.k2.p: How many independent judges a swarm of N correlated agents is worth.
research.k3.p: Page's exact identity for numeric tasks. It splits a crowd's accuracy into competence and diversity with no modelling assumptions.
research.k3.formula: crowd error = mean individual error − diversity
research.k4.p: AUC and Brier score. A thresholded F1 alone can't tell a cautious agent from a wrong one.
research.k5.p: A swarm that needs hundreds of calls for one answer has to earn them.
research.papers.note: Working titles are marked as such. Planned work lists its design, never results.
research.p1.p: An exploratory pilot. People and LLM agents rate the same emails for fraud. The best individual is an agent and the best crowd is human. Sampling temperature alone doesn't give agents the disagreement a crowd needs.
research.p2.p: Two studies. The first splits the evidence of a fraud case between agents and sweeps the overlap from disjoint to identical, expecting accuracy to peak in between. The second tests whether Portuguese-native and global models fail on different Brazilian scams.
research.p3.p: Persona-based forecasting with post-stratification, aimed at municipal swing and runoff vote transfer in the 2026 general election, with baselines and hypotheses fixed before the outcome.
research.p4.h: Hybrid human and AI collectives: error complementarity
research.p4.p: If people and agents make different kinds of mistakes, a mixed crowd should beat both.
research.p5.h: Monoculture risk: correlated attacks on swarms
research.p5.p: Prompt injections embedded in fraudulent emails, single-lineage swarms against mixed ones, and median against robust aggregation.
research.p6.p: Does diversity induced by activation steering lower error correlation as much as adding a second model family, and what does each cost? This is our first company experiment.
research.p7.p: A swarm forecasts Brazilian inflation, interest and exchange rates each week, benchmarked against the Banco Central's survey of professional forecasters. The questions are future-dated, so training data can't leak the answers.
research.r1.p: Forecasts are hashed and timestamped before the result is known.
research.r2.p: Every level of granularity has an error no model can beat. We report skill above it, never against zero.
research.r3.p: A faithful structure with no predictive gain is a finding, and we commit to publishing it in advance.
research.r4.p: Refusals, hedges and ideological lean are logged and reported as properties of the models, never as findings about people.
research.r5.p: Every synthetic output is labelled as one. Nothing electoral leaves the lab before polls close.

post.effective-crowd-size.title: A thousand agents, about four opinions
post.effective-crowd-size.summary: Effective crowd size turns “our agents mostly agree” into a number, and puts a hard ceiling on what adding agents can buy.
post.copies-and-strangers.title: Why five good copies lose to five decent strangers
post.copies-and-strangers.summary: A crowd of strong agents can lose to a crowd of weaker, more varied judges. A small worked example shows how.
post.built-not-sampled.title: Built, not sampled
post.built-not-sampled.summary: Surowiecki listed four conditions for a wise crowd. Most agent swarms meet one. Our second paper is about the other three.
post.where-polls-cannot-see.title: Where polls cannot see
post.where-polls-cannot-see.summary: Design notes for Model Society: why we don't chase the national number, and what a language model is allowed to contribute.
post.one-injection-every-agent.title: One injection, every agent
post.one-injection-every-agent.summary: Diversity is usually sold as an accuracy boost. In a swarm it's also a security property.

post.why-a-bee.summary: The iraí is small, stingless, urban, and careful about its entrance.

about.meta_desc: IRAI is a Brazilian research company that measures and engineers the collective intelligence of AI swarms. It is named after the iraí, a stingless bee.
about.lede: IRAI is a Brazilian research company that measures and engineers the collective intelligence of AI swarms.
about.name.h2: Named after a bee that locks its door at night
about.name.p1_html: The iraí, Nannotrigona testaceicornis, is a stingless bee a few millimetres long, black with grey hairs, at home in hollow bricks and stone walls across Brazilian cities. Its name is usually read from Tupi as “river of honey”.
about.name.p2: Every evening the colony seals its wax entrance tube. Every morning it opens it again. Guards stay around the entrance through the day.
about.name.p3: We liked three things about it. A colony is many small workers with different jobs, which is our thesis about swarms. The guards are our safety work. And the name ends in AI.
about.company.p1_html: IRAI grows out of ICIA, a research programme on how the collective intelligence of human crowds emerges in swarms of language models. Its first paper, Echoes of Humanity, was presented at AMCIS 2026.
about.company.p2: What that programme found is why the company exists. Run one model a thousand times and you still have one opinion.
about.dont.p: We don't sell orchestration, and we won't tell you to add agents. We count the independent judges in the swarm you have, on whatever framework you run.
foot.about: We measure how well AI swarms think as a group. Made in Brazil.
foot.door_note: The iraí seals its nest at nightfall and opens it at dawn. This site does the same on Brasília time: the entrance is open from 06:00 to 18:00 in São Paulo.
foot.fine: Synthetic simulations published by IRAI are research outputs, never electoral polls.
